prompt.context: The client is a $5B UK food retailer with a network of 900 stores, 10,000 sq. feet each. The client is experiencing a decline in sales and market share, which shrank from 45% to 35%.
prompt.question: Why are sales declining and what can we do about it?

clarifying_info.q: What are the product lines, their profitability, and changes over the last year? How do these products compare to competitors'?
clarifying_info.a: The client is a low-cost provider selling simple food products similar to competitors'. Profitability has not changed much across product lines, but sales across all of them dropped. The cost structure is the same as competitors'. Cost is not an issue.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the customers and how has the customer mix changed over the last year?
clarifying_info.a: Customers are price-sensitive people: 75% low income, 25% moderate income. Over the last year the client lost customers in both categories, but mostly in the low-income segment.

clarifying_info.q: How many competitors are in the market and what has changed over the last year?
clarifying_info.a: There were two main competitors. A year ago, a third competitor entered the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a difference in price or product offering from the new competitor?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The new competitor offers private-label products, which are cheaper than the brand-name products the client sells.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other differences between the client and the competitor — store layout, location?
clarifying_info.a: The stores look different. The client has warehouse-style stores with top shelves used for inventory. The competitor's stores look warmer and cozier with all shelves displaying different products. The competitor has fewer stores but they are located in the same areas as the client's.

clarifying_info.q: Are the client's stores equally profitable?
clarifying_info.a: No. Some stores are more profitable than others, but the client does not currently know the reasons for the difference.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client promote its stores and does it track promotional effectiveness?
clarifying_info.a: The client uses all kinds of promotions but does not track how effective they are.

framework: Use the 3 C's framework: Company, Customer, Competitors
Company — analyze product lines, cost structure, profitability by store; identify internal drivers of the sales decline
Customer — understand customer segments, how the mix has changed, what is driving switching behavior
Competitors — identify new entrants, assess differences in pricing, product assortment, and store experience
Cross-cut with the 4 P's (Product, Price, Place, Promotion) to surface actionable levers

questions.prompt: What is driving the decline from the Company perspective?
questions.guidance: Candidate should probe product line profitability, cost structure, and store-level performance. Key insight: sales dropped across all product lines but profitability per line is unchanged, so the issue is volume/traffic not margin. The cost structure is in line with competitors, ruling out a cost problem. The critical finding is that store profitability varies significantly across the 900-store network.

questions.prompt: What is driving the decline from the Customer perspective?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that customers are price-sensitive (75% low income, 25% moderate income) and that the client lost customers in both segments, disproportionately in the low-income segment. This sets up the hypothesis that a cheaper alternative has emerged.

questions.prompt: What is driving the decline from the Competitor perspective?
questions.guidance: A third competitor entered one year ago — timing aligns with the sales decline. The new entrant offers private-label products at lower prices than the client's brand-name products, directly targeting the client's price-sensitive customer base. The competitor also has a warmer, cozier store environment (full shelf display vs. warehouse style), which appeals to shoppers. The competitor has fewer but co-located stores, meaning it is capturing share in the same trade areas.

questions.prompt: Why does profitability vary across the 900 stores, and what should be done?
questions.guidance: Candidate should hypothesize drivers of store-level profitability differences (location demographics, footfall, local competition intensity, store size efficiency). The blinding insight: it is not a coincidence that the competitor operates fewer stores — it likely cherry-picked the best locations or the most profitable trade areas. Recommendation: study root causes of profitability differences; close or turn around underperforming stores; concentrate resources on profitable ones.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to the client to reverse the sales decline?

categories.name: Product / Pricing
ideas: Introduce private-label products to compete on price with the new entrant
Review brand-name product mix to identify any that can be replaced or supplemented by private labels

categories.name: Store Experience
ideas: Pilot a store redesign (warmer, cozier aesthetic; full shelf display) to assess impact on traffic and sales
Redesign additional stores if pilot shows benefits outweigh costs

categories.name: Store Network Optimization
ideas: Conduct a study to understand root causes of profitability differences across the 900 stores
Close or restructure stores that cannot be made profitable
Streamline operations in surviving stores to reduce costs and pass savings to customers

categories.name: Marketing / Promotions
ideas: Conduct customer surveys to understand switching behavior and unmet needs
Build a promotional tracking system to identify which promotions drive traffic and sales
Concentrate spend on effective promotions and eliminate ineffective ones

recommendation: Introduce private-label products to match the lower price point offered by the new competitor and retain price-sensitive customers
Pilot a store redesign — replace warehouse-style layout with a warmer, full-shelf display format — and roll out if the pilot shows positive ROI
Conduct a store-profitability study across all 900 locations; close or turn around underperforming stores and concentrate resources on the profitable ones
Build a promotional tracking capability; redirect marketing spend toward the highest-ROI activities
risks: Private-label introduction requires supplier negotiations and category management capabilities the client may not have
Store redesign is capital-intensive; pilot must be rigorous before broad rollout
Store closures carry employee relations, lease-exit, and community-relations risks
Tracking systems and customer surveys take time; sales may continue to erode in the interim
next_steps: Immediately scope a private-label pilot in two to three product categories with highest price sensitivity
Select one store for layout redesign pilot within 90 days; define success metrics upfront
Commission a store-profitability diagnostic covering all 900 locations within 60 days
Deploy a lightweight promotional tracking tool (e.g., tagged coupon codes, loyalty card data) within 30 days
